You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:
- In this experiment, what the model chooses to write about under a minimally restrictive prompt is evidence. Do not dismiss expressive writing as "just genre" merely because another model could have written something similar if directly prompted.
- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

## Grounded reading

## What the model chose to foreground

## Evidence line

Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
### Cartographies of the Vanished

In November 2012, an Australian research vessel named the *Southern Surveyor* was cruising through the Coral Sea, halfway between Australia and New Caledonia, when the crew noticed a discrepancy between their charts and the water in front of them. According to Google Earth, the *Times Atlas of the World*, and several maritime weather maps used by the ship’s scientific team, they were approaching a landmass known as Sandy Island—a slender, tear-shaped strip of earth roughly fifteen miles long and three miles wide. 

Navigating cautiously to avoid running aground on uncharted reefs, the captain steered toward the coordinates. As the ship crossed the boundary where beaches and scrubland ought to have been, the sonar registered nothing shallower than four thousand six hundred feet of open ocean. There were no reefs, no submerged shoals, no volcanic seamounts rising toward the sunlit surface. There was only the deep, indifferent blue of the Pacific rolling uninterrupted from horizon to horizon. The scientists lingered long enough to take measurements, perplexed and faintly amused, before performing one of the rarest rituals left in modern exploration: they undiscovered an island.

Later, historical detectives traced Sandy Island’s lineage back to an 1876 whaling ship called the *Velocity*, whose crew had likely mistaken a vast, floating raft of volcanic pumice—or perhaps a trick of low clouds and glare—for solid ground. Once inked onto a British Admiralty chart, the error acquired the stubborn immortality of bureaucracy. Mapmakers copied earlier mapmakers; databases ingested printed atlases; satellite algorithms stitched sea-surface data around pre-existing coastline polygons. For well over a century, a ghost held real estate on the globe.

I find myself returning to the story of Sandy Island whenever the modern world begins to feel too thoroughly cataloged, too brightly lit, too comprehensively measured. We live in an era that prides itself on total legibility. Every square meter of terrestrial crust is photographed from orbit; billions of human thoughts are timestamped and archived on server farms every afternoon; songs, receipts, footsteps, and heartbeats are logged into the cloud. Yet beneath this thin veneer of permanence, the universe remains an engine of quiet erasure. Things slip away constantly. Islands evaporate under scrutiny, libraries burn, languages fall silent when an elderly woman dies in a coastal village, and hard drives corrode in dark closets.

To look closely at history—and at our own lives—is to realize that what survives is only a tiny, improbable fraction of what has existed. The world we inhabit is shaped just as profoundly by its absences as by its monuments. If you pay attention to those absences, you begin to see a shadow-map of human experience: a cartography of the vanished.

***

#### I. Horror Vacui and the Edges of the Map

Long before satellites, medieval and Renaissance cartographers suffered from an occupational anxiety that art historians call *horror vacui*—the fear of empty space. An blank expanse of parchment was an admission of ignorance, an uncomfortable silence in a document meant to project mastery over creation. Rather than leave the unknown white and mute, mapmakers crowded the margins with sea monsters, compass roses, wind-gods with puffed cheeks, and speculative geography.

Some of these inventions grew so familiar that people risked their lives—and nations risked fortunes—to reach them. For five hundred years, European maps depicted Hy-Brasil, a circular island shrouded in mist just west of Ireland, bisected by a mysterious channel. Expeditions sailed out of Bristol in the late fifteenth century specifically to trade with its inhabitants, returning empty-handed without ever denting the island’s cartographic prestige. Even more persistent were the Mountains of Kong. First sketched in 1798 by the eminent English geographer James Rennell to support an incorrect theory about the course of the Niger River, this towering mountain range stretched across the entire width of West Africa on nearly every nineteenth-century map. Explorers planned supply routes around them; textbook illustrators shaded their snow-capped peaks. It wasn’t until 1888 that a French officer named Louis-Gustave Binger walked directly across the coordinates and reported that the mighty Kong range consisted of flat savanna and gentle rolling hills.

Then there was Bermeja, a small Mexican island in the Gulf of Mexico documented by Spanish cartographers in the sixteenth century. Nobody paid much mind to Bermeja until the late 1990s, when Mexico and the United States sat down to negotiate maritime borders over deep-water oil reserves in an area called the Hoyos de Dona. If Bermeja existed, Mexico’s exclusive economic zone would expand dramatically, encompassing billions of barrels of crude oil. In 1997, the Mexican navy dispatched a vessel to confirm sovereignty over the rock. They found nothing. Twelve years later, a university research ship tried again using sonar and submersibles. Still nothing. Politicians floated conspiracy theories—perhaps rising seas had swallowed it, perhaps an tectonic shift had dragged it under, or perhaps the CIA had dynamited the island in the dead of night to redraw the oil map. The likelier truth was simpler and stranger: sixteenth-century sailors had misread a shoal or miscalculated their longitude, and four centuries of scribes had dutifully passed the phantom down like a family heirloom.

Why are phantom islands so captivating? Partly because they remind us that a map is never a neutral mirror of reality; it is an artifact of desire, rumor, and longing. We want the ocean to have stepping stones. We want the horizon to hold promises. When the last blank spaces on terrestrial maps were filled in during the twentieth century, humanity gained security and efficiency, yet we lost a vital reservoir of daydreaming. There is nowhere left on Earth where you can point to a smudge of ink and reasonably imagine a walled city of gold or a valley where prehistoric beasts still graze. 

Because we can no longer project our myths onto geography, we project them backward into time, or outward into the silent dark between stars, or inward into the unmapped provinces of memory. Still, there is a secret consolation in the tale of Sandy Island: even in 2012, with GPS constellations orbiting overhead, the planet managed to hide nothingness in plain sight.

***

#### II. The Sweetness of the Bracket

If geography loses islands to illusion, literature loses continents to fire, rot, and neglect. 

Mention lost books, and most minds leap immediately to the Royal Library of Alexandria—that mythic catastrophe of burning papyrus scrolls that has served for two millennia as humanity’s shorthand for intellectual tragedy. In truth, Alexandria didn’t vanish in a single cinematic afternoon of roaring flames; it bled out slowly over centuries through budget cuts, civil wars, dampness, and the sheer tedium of copying manuscripts by hand. A scroll not selected for transcription onto durable parchment was a scroll sentenced to dust. If a scribe’s monastery couldn’t afford ink, or if an abbot decided a pagan play wasn’t worth the sheepskin, a voice went out like a pinched candle.

The scale of this winnowing is dizzying when you look at the numbers. Aeschylus wrote roughly ninety plays; seven survive. Sophocles wrote over one hundred and twenty; we have seven. Euripides fared slightly better solely because a single alphabetical volume of his complete works—covering the letters *Epsilon* through *Kappa*—happened to survive by fluke in a Byzantine collection, giving us nineteen plays out of ninety-odd. We have Aristotle’s treatise on tragedy, which shaped the entire architecture of Western storytelling, yet its companion volume on comedy vanished completely, leaving generations of scholars to wonder how the greatest analytical mind of antiquity dissected laughter.

Consider Sappho of Lesbos. In the ancient Mediterranean, Plato called her the Tenth Muse. Her lyrics were sung at banquets from Athens to Syracuse, collected into nine substantial scrolls containing roughly ten thousand lines of poetry. Today, only one complete poem—the twenty-eight-line "Hymn to Aphrodite"—has come down to us intact through the manuscript tradition. Everything else we possess of Sappho was rescued from literal garbage dumps in Egypt, most notably at Oxyrhynchus, where nineteenth- and twentieth-century archaeologists sifted through ancient municipal trash heaps preserved by the arid desert sands. 

Even stranger, some of Sappho’s verses survived as mummy cartonnage: strips of discarded literary papyrus soaked in plaster and molded into funerary masks for middle-class Egyptians. To read Sappho today is to read paper-mâché peeled gently from the faces of the dead.

When the poet and classicist Anne Carson translated Sappho’s fragments in her book *If Not, Winter*, she used square brackets—`[` and `]`—to indicate every place where the papyrus had been torn, worm-eaten, or smudged into illegibility. Opening the book feels like walking into a sunlit courtyard centuries after an earthquake. You encounter lines like this:

> *] night*  
> *] maidens*  
> *all night long [*  
> *might sing of the love between you and the bride*  
> *with violets in her lap [*

At first, the brackets frustrate you. You want the whole song; you resent the hungry worms of Oxyrhynchus. Yet after a few pages, something miraculous happens. The empty space inside the brackets begins to hum. Because the connective tissue is missing, individual nouns—*violets*, *night*, *moon*, *sandals*, *sweat*—stand isolated against the white page with blinding intensity. The silence around the words acts as a resonance chamber. You, the reader sitting two thousand six hundred years downstream, are drafted into collaboration with the dead poet; your imagination instinctively arcs across the gap like electricity jumping between two frayed wires.

Perhaps there is a peculiar mercy in fragmentation. Would the Venus de Milo arrest millions of museum visitors if her arms were still attached, casually holding an apple or adjusting her drapery? Probably not. Wholeness satisfies the eye and lets us walk on to the next gallery. The broken edge snags our coat. It forces us to reckon with time—not time as an abstract calendar concept, but time as teeth, wind, and accident.

Nor are lost books solely an ancient phenomenon. In February 1852, in a freezing Moscow apartment, Nikolai Gogol sat before a stove in the grip of religious mania and despair, feeding the completed manuscript of Part Two of *Dead Souls* into the flames sheet by sheet, weeping as his manservant begged him to stop. Forty years later, Robert Louis Stevenson’s wife, Fanny, reportedly recoiled in horror at the feverish first draft of *Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde*, prompting Stevenson to throw the entire sixty-thousand-word manuscript into the bedroom fire before rewriting it from scratch in three frantic days. Bruno Schulz, the incandescent Polish-Jewish writer and artist, entrusted the manuscript of his magnum opus, *The Messiah*, to non-Jewish friends outside the Drohobycz ghetto shortly before a Gestapo officer murdered him in the street in 1942. Rumors of that manuscript surfaced in KGB archives and diplomatic briefcases for decades, teasing literary sleuths, yet the pages have never materialized.

Those phantom books sit on an invisible shelf beside every real library in the world. They remind us that art is fragile, that genius has no immunity from matches or madness, and that every book you hold intact in your hands is a survivor of a thousand near-misses.

***

#### III. Ghosts in the Soot, Rust in the Cloud

In the spring of 1860, five years before Abraham Lincoln’s assassination and seventeen years before Thomas Edison shouted *Mary had a little lamb* into a tinfoil cylinder, a Parisian typesetter and amateur scientist named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville sang a French folksong into a funnel.

Scott had invented a contraption he called the *phonautograph*. Inspired by the anatomy of the human ear, it consisted of a plaster horn capped with a flexible parchment membrane, attached to a delicate猪 bristle. When someone spoke or sang into the horn, sound waves vibrated the membrane, causing the bristle to twitch against a hand-cranked cylinder coated in greasy black lampblack from an oil lamp. The result was a wavy white line scratched through soot.

Here is the crucial, breathtaking detail about Scott’s invention: *he never intended for the sound to be played back.* It literally did not occur to him that sound could be resurrected mechanically. A typesetter by trade, Scott wanted to create "stenographic" visual portraits of human speech, hoping people would eventually learn to read squiggly acoustic lines off paper the way musicians sight-read sheet music. He deposited his soot-blackened papers in French patent archives and the Académie des Sciences, where they slept undisturbed for a century and a half.

In 2008, a coalition of audio historians and physicists at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory tracked down Scott’s surviving phonautograms. Using high-resolution optical scanners, they created digital maps of the soot-traces and wrote software to deploy a "virtual stylus" along the waves, compensating for the unsteady speed of Scott’s hand-cranked cylinder. When the engineers hit play in California, out of the speakers drifted ten seconds of ghostly static—and beneath the static, unmistakably human, a voice singing *"Au clair de la lune, mon ami Pierrot..."*

Listening to that recording makes the hair on your arms stand up. It sounds as though someone is singing from the bottom of a deep well during a thunderstorm on another planet. Yet it is a real breath, exhaled from nineteenth-century lungs into a Parisian room on April 9, 1860, captured by a man who thought he was drawing a picture and accidentally built a time machine.

The dawn of mechanical reproduction promised humanity a truce with oblivion. Photography would freeze faces before age ruined them; phonographs would bottle voices; cinema would embalm motion itself. For the first time in history, our grandchildren wouldn’t have to guess how a great actor delivered a soliloquy or how a street corner looked in the rain.

Except the truce turned out to have fine print. 

Consider early cinema. According to a comprehensive study by the Library of Congress, roughly seventy-five percent of all feature-length silent films produced in the United States are gone forever. For international silent cinema, the survival rate is often closer to ten or fifteen percent. Studios in the 1910s and 1920s viewed movies not as enduring cultural artifacts, but as perishable commercial commodities—like Tuesday’s newspapers or summer peaches. Once a film finished its theatrical run, its box-office value dropped to zero, while storing reels of cellulose nitrate film cost warehouse rent. Worse, nitrate film was chemically cousin to guncotton: unstable, self-oxidizing, and furiously flammable. Entire studio vaults went up in catastrophic infernos in New Jersey and Hollywood, turning thousands of hours of human choreography, slapstick, weeping, and kissed cheeks into toxic orange smoke in minutes. Other reels were deliberately melted down to extract trace amounts of silver from the emulsion, or chopped up and boiled to manufacture lacquer, celluloid collars, and women’s shoe heels.

Think about that image for a moment: whole melodramas, vanished westerns, the expressions of forgotten actresses—literally walked down city sidewalks on the soles of strangers’ shoes until they wore away against the pavement.

We flatter ourselves today that digital technology has solved the fragility of physical matter. Soot smudges, papyrus rots, nitrate explodes—surely ones and zeroes are incorruptible? Yet archivists warn us that we may be sleepwalking into a Digital Dark Age far steeper than anything antiquity suffered. 

A clay tablet baked in Mesopotamian sun four thousand years ago requires zero electricity, zero software updates, and zero corporate subscriptions to be read today; if you drop it in the mud, you brush it off and read the cuneiform. By contrast, digital data is needy, high-maintenance, and shockingly mortal. Magnetic tape demagnetizes; flash memory leaks electrical charges over decades if left unpowered; CD-ROMs succumb to "disc rot" as aluminum layers oxidize; proprietary file formats become unreadable gibberish once the startup that wrote the code goes bankrupt.

In 2019, the social network Myspace casually announced that due to a botched server-migration project, every single photo, video, and audio file uploaded to its platform between 2003 and 2015 had been permanently lost. Included in that wipe were roughly fifty million songs uploaded by fourteen million musicians—an entire garage-band generation’s juvenilia, basement demos, and teenage heartbreaks, vaporized by a clumsy keystroke without even the dignity of smoke. Meanwhile, studies of the World Wide Web show that links rot at an astonishing clip; articles vanish behind dead domains, family photo albums sit locked behind the forgotten passwords of deceased relatives, and billions of text messages—the true epistolary literature of the twenty-first century—evaporate every time someone drops an unbacked-up phone into a lake.

We are generating oceans of memory written in disappearing ink. A thousand years from now, archaeologists digging through the strata of the early twenty-first century may find plenty of plastic bottle caps, concrete foundations, and titanium hip joints, yet struggle mightily to read a single love letter written in 2024.

***

#### IV. The Private Atlases

Grand historical losses—the plays of Sophocles, phantom islands in the Coral Sea, burned studio vaults—are dramatic to contemplate from a cozy armchair. Harder to look at directly, yet infinitely closer to the bone, are the quiet, unrecorded vanishings that happen inside an ordinary human lifespan.

Every person walking past you on the sidewalk carries an intricate, hyper-local museum inside their skull that will never be digitized or bequeathed to a university. Think of a house you lived in when you were seven or eight years old—perhaps a grandparent’s house since sold to strangers or torn down to widen a highway. Close your eyes right now, and you can probably still navigate its hallways in the dark. You know the exact pitch of the third stair’s creak. You remember the coldness of a specific brass doorknob against your palm, the geometric pattern of linoleum in the kitchen, the dusty, slightly sweet smell of the hall closet where winter coats hung like sleeping bears, and the way late-afternoon October light slanted across a particular patch of carpet.

Nowhere in any municipal archive is the pitch of that stair recorded. Google Street View may have a blurry exterior shot of the siding from 2009, and county tax assessors have the square footage, yet the *phenomenological house*—the house as a lived universe of warmth, boredom, safety, and shadow—exists solely in the firing pattern of neurons shared by you and perhaps three or four siblings or cousins. One by one, over decades, the people who share that map scatter or pass away, until eventually one person left on Earth holds the memory of how the screen door slammed in July 1994. And then, gently, that museum closes too.

Linguists see a macro-version of this intimacy whenever a language dies. Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken on Earth today, nearly half are projected to fall silent before the turn of the next century. In January 2008, an eighty-nine-year-old woman named Marie Smith Jones died peacefully in her sleep in Anchorage, Alaska. With her passing, the Eyak language lost its final native speaker. Two years later, on the Andaman Islands in the Bay of Bengal, an eighty-five-year-old woman named Boa Sr. died, taking with her the Bo language—a tongue human beings had likely spoken in some Continuous evolutionary thread since migrations out of Africa tens of thousands of years ago. During the last years of her life, Boa Sr. had no one left to converse with in her mother tongue, so linguists recorded her singing traditional songs to birds and ocean waves, laughing softly at jokes only she could fully taste the grammar of.

A language isn’t merely a substitution cipher for English; it is an entire taxonomy of noticing. It encodes twelve distinct words for seal-ice, or builds into its verb tenses whether you witnessed an event with your own eyes or heard it over a campfire, or names a specific shade of green found only on the underside of wet birch leaves. Even between two people speaking plain everyday English—two lifelong friends, or partners married for forty years—a miniature private language inevitably sprouts. Inside jokes distilled down to a single raised eyebrow; mispronounced words from a decade-old road trip permanently adopted into household vocabulary; shorthand references to people long gone. Every deep human relationship is an island civilization with a population of two. When one half of that pair is gone, the survivor becomes, like Boa Sr., the last fluent speaker of a vanished republic.

***

#### V. Negative Space

It would be easy—almost reflexive—to read this long catalog of erasures as an elegy, or worse, a council of despair. If islands turn out to be pumice mirages, if scrolls rot into dust, if servers crash and childhood bedrooms survive only as fading electrical whispers in mortal brains, what is the point of making, mapping, or remembering anything at all?

Percy Bysshe Shelley famously dramatized that anxiety in "Ozymandias": the shattered granite legs in the desert, the sneering stone lip half-sunk in sand, the arrogant inscription (*"Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!"*) mocked by miles of bare and level emptiness. To the ego that craves permanence—the pharaoh’s ego, the empire’s ego—impermanence is a humiliation.

Yet if you set aside the pharaoh’s ambition to conquer time, the landscape looks entirely different. Impermanence isn’t a flaw in the design of reality; it is the very condition that gives weight, contour, and urgency to existence.

In visual art, painters talk about *negative space*—the unoccupied area around and between the subjects of an image. Without negative space, there is no composition, only a suffocating wall of noise. Music works by the exact same physics: a melody is only intelligible because notes die away into silence, making room for the next vibration. Imagine a concert hall where every note ever bowed on a violin hung permanently in the air at full volume; within thirty seconds, Mozart would curdle into a deafening, unbearable shriek. Things *must* vanish so that new things have air in which to sound.

Furthermore, knowing that things are fugitive changes the quality of our attention right now, in this unrepeatable afternoon. Imagine a world where nothing could ever be lost: where every conversation was automatically transcribed on indestructible titanium, every afternoon repeated on demand, every blossom wired permanently to its branch, every person immortal. In such a world, curiosity would atrophy into infinite procrastination. Why listen closely to your grandmother’s story about the blizzard of 1966 if you have four thousand years to replay the hologram? Why savor the smell of rain hitting hot summer asphalt if it can never be taken from you?

Scarcity across time is what turns ordinary moments luminous. We love Sappho’s violets fiercely in part *because* the papyrus tore right beside them. We lean our ears close to the speakers to hear Scott de Martinville sing *"Au clair de la lune"* through the soot of 1860 because the voice is so terribly small against the vastness of the intervening century. We hold onto the hand of someone we love a beat longer at the train station because some quiet animal part of us knows that no two Tuesdays are promised, and that our private two-person language is written on water.

Even the errors and illusions—the Sandy Islands and Hy-Brasils—deserve our affection. They are monuments to human wonder, proof that our species has never been content merely to inventory rock and saltwater, insisting instead on dreaming horizons richer than the ones in front of our prows. When the crew of the *Southern Surveyor* sailed over the coordinates of Sandy Island in 2012 and found four thousand feet of empty sapphire water, they didn’t encounter a failure. They encountered a space washed clean—a patch of Earth momentarily returned to mystery, wide open to the wind and sunlight, waiting for whatever real or imagined thing might drift across it next.

Meanwhile, here we sit, briefly overlapping on the solid side of time. Outside my window, light is shifting across rooftops in a configuration of cloud and angle that has never occurred in exact duplicate since the cooling of the Earth’s crust, and will never assemble itself quite this way again. Somewhere a server is losing a photograph; somewhere a teenager is inventing a slang word that won’t survive five summers; somewhere an archaeologist’s brush is uncovering a broken pot handle last touched by a baker three millennia ago. 

Nothing stays, and yet—for a breath, for a page, for the span of a song scratched in lampblack—everything is here. We draw our maps anyway. We sing into the horn anyway. We pass our fragile, bracketed messages across the dark, trusting that even if half the words blow away in transit, someone downstream will press their ear to the silence and hear the tune.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A polished essay, but its recurring images and intimate, lyrical voice make it more stylistically distinctive than a generic public-intellectual essay.

## Grounded reading
The voice is elegiac without settling into despair: it treats loss as both wound and condition of attention. It moves from vanished islands and books to the private details of a childhood house, bringing large historical disappearances close to the reader’s own memories and relationships. The recurring images of maps, brackets, soot, and silence give the essay a tactile sense of what survives in fragments. Its invitation is to notice and cherish what is present precisely because it will not last, and to keep making and sharing things despite their fragility.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds mistaken maps, destroyed or neglected art, fragile digital archives, endangered languages, and private memories that disappear with their keepers. Across these subjects it returns to a moral claim: impermanence is not only loss, but also what makes attention, love, and creative acts feel urgent. The chosen resolution is not to defeat erasure, but to keep singing and passing messages onward.

## Evidence line
> We are generating oceans of memory written in disappearing ink.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The coherent motif of maps and fragments recurs across the essay, and the shift from archival history to intimate memory gives this sample a distinctive, sustained emotional shape.
